facts.statement: Daliansaurus was a small troodontid theropod dinosaur about 1 meter long that lived in China during the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Daliansaurus (meaning "Dalian reptile") is a genus of small troodontid theropod dinosaur, measuring approximately 1 m long, from the Early Cretaceous of China.

facts.statement: The genus contains the single species Daliansaurus liaoningensis, which was named in 2017 based on a nearly complete skeleton.
facts.quote: It contains a single species, D. liaoningensis, named in 2017 by Shen and colleagues from a nearly complete skeleton preserved in three dimensions.

facts.statement: Daliansaurus is unusual for having an enlarged claw on the fourth toe in addition to the typical sickle claw on the second toe.
facts.quote: Daliansaurus is unusual in possessing an enlarged claw on the fourth digit of the foot, in addition to the "sickle claw" found on the second digit of the feet of most paravians.

facts.statement: Daliansaurus possessed long metatarsal bones and bird-like uncinate processes, a feature previously unknown among troodontids.
facts.quote: It also has long metatarsal bones, and apparently possesses bird-like uncinate processes (a first among troodontids).

facts.statement: Daliansaurus was a small, lightly built, and likely feathered dinosaur about 1 meter long, similar in size to Sinovenator and Sinusonasus.
facts.quote: Daliansaurus is a small, lightly-built, and most likely feathered troodontid measuring approximately 1 m in length, similar in size to Sinovenator and Sinusonasus.

facts.statement: The skull of Daliansaurus measured 13.8 cm in length and was proportionally larger than that of Mei.
facts.quote: The skull of Daliansaurus, which measures 13.8 cm long, is proportionally larger than that of Mei.

facts.statement: The four front teeth in Daliansaurus's upper jaw were D-shaped rather than recurved.
facts.quote: The four premaxillary teeth are not recurved but D-shaped.

facts.statement: Ribs on two dorsal vertebrae of Daliansaurus bore uncinate processes, curved projections similar to those seen in Velociraptor and other dinosaurs.
facts.quote: The ribs of two of the dorsal vertebrae unusually appear to bear uncinate processes, in the form of curved and rod-like projections similar to those of Velociraptor, Linheraptor, and Heyuannia.

facts.statement: Daliansaurus is best distinguished among troodontids by a large claw on the fourth toe of its foot.
facts.quote: Among troodontids, Daliansaurus is best distinguished by the large claw on the fourth (outermost) digit of its foot.

facts.statement: The claw on Daliansaurus's fourth toe was the same length as its second toe claw but was considerably more robust.
facts.quote: While troodontids are well known for the sickle-like claws on the second digits of their feet, the claw on the fourth digit of Daliansaurus is the same length as the second, and is also considerably more robust.

facts.statement: Daliansaurus had proportionally much longer metatarsal bones than other troodontids.
facts.quote: Proportionally, Daliansaurus has much longer metatarsal bones than other troodontids.

facts.statement: Daliansaurus lived in the volcanically influenced, cold climate of the Lujiatun Beds alongside relatives like Sinovenator, Sinusonasus, and Mei.
facts.quote: In the Lujiatun Beds of the Yixian Formation, a volcanically-influenced region with a cold climate, Daliansaurus lived alongside its closest relatives - Sinovenator, Sinusonasus, and Mei, with which it forms the group Sinovenatorinae.

facts.statement: The fossil was found in Early Cretaceous volcanic deposits about 126 million years old in the village of Lujiatun, Liaoning, China.
facts.quote: The specimen was found in Early Cretaceous (~126 Ma old, dating to the Barremian epoch) volcanic deposits of the Lujiatun Beds of the Yixian Formation, in the village of Lujiatun near Beipiao, Liaoning, China.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen is stored at the Dalian Natural History Museum under the number DNHM D2885.
facts.quote: It is stored in the Dalian Natural History Museum (DNHM) in Dalian, Liaoning, under the specimen number DNHM D2885.

facts.statement: Daliansaurus was formally described in 2017 by a team including Shen Caizhi, Lü Junchang, Liu Sizhao, Martin Kundrát, Stephen Brusatte, and Gao Hailong.
facts.quote: In 2017, DNHM D2885 was described in a research paper published in Acta Geologica Sinica and authored by Shen Caizhi, Lü Junchang, Liu Sizhao, Martin Kundrát, Stephen Brusatte, and Gao Hailong.

facts.statement: Daliansaurus belongs to the Troodontidae family, a group of paravian dinosaurs known for sickle claws on the second toe.
facts.quote: Daliansaurus is unusual in possessing an enlarged claw on the fourth digit of the foot, in addition to the "sickle claw" found on the second digit of the feet of most paravians.

facts.statement: Daliansaurus is part of the subgroup Sinovenatorinae, which also includes Mei, Sinovenator, and Sinusonasus, though the defining trait of this group is not present in Daliansaurus.
facts.quote: The analysis also found that Daliansaurus formed a distinct evolutionary radiation along with other troodontids in the Yixian Formation: Mei, Sinovenator, and Sinusonasus. This group, which was named the Sinovenatorinae, was united by a synapomorphy not observable for Daliansaurus, the possession of a wide and flattened fourth metatarsal.

facts.statement: Daliansaurus is known from a single nearly complete skeleton, though parts like the back of the skull and rear lower jaw were reconstructed and are not original fossil material.
facts.quote: Daliansaurus is known from a single nearly-complete skeleton preserved in three dimensions. Parts of the specimen had been reconstructed and do not represent genuine fossil material, including the back of the skull and the rear portion of the lower jaw.

facts.statement: The preserved posture of the Daliansaurus fossil shows the head and neck curled backward, the tail curved forward, and the arms positioned asymmetrically.
facts.quote: The head and neck of the fossil are curled backwards, while the tail itself is curved forwards; the left arm is extended while the right arm is tucked inwards.

facts.statement: Daliansaurus likely had superior running abilities compared to other troodontids due to its long metatarsals.
facts.quote: The long metatarsals present in Daliansaurus suggest that its running capabilities were better-developed than those of other troodontids.

facts.statement: Uncinate processes on Daliansaurus ribs may have reinforced its rib cage and improved breathing efficiency, similar to modern birds.
facts.quote: the possible presence of uncinate processes on its ribs would have provided reinforcement for the rib cage, as well as an increase in the effectiveness of the muscles involved in breathing, as in modern birds.

facts.statement: Daliansaurus is unusual for having an enlarged claw on its fourth toe, in addition to the 'killing claw' on its second toe.
facts.quote: Daliansaurus es inusual al poseer una garra agrandada en el cuarto dedo del pie, en adición a la "garra asesina" que se halla en el segundo dedo del pie en este y muchos otros paravianos.

facts.statement: Daliansaurus appears to be the first troodontid known to possess a bird-like uncinate process.
facts.quote: aparentemente posee un proceso uncinado de aspecto similar a un ave, el primero entre los troodóntidos.

facts.statement: Daliansaurus lived approximately 125 million years ago during the Early Cretaceous (Barremian) in what is now Asia.
facts.quote: vivió hace aproximadamente 125 millones de años a principios periodo Cretácico durante el Barremiense en lo que es hoy Asia.

facts.statement: The genus Daliansaurus was established by Shen et al. in 2017.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Shen et al., 2017

facts.statement: The species Daliansaurus liaoningensis was described by Shen et al. in 2017.
facts.quote: species_authority: Shen et al., 2017

facts.statement: Daliansaurus lived in the Lujiatun Beds of the Yixian Formation alongside other sinovenatorines like Sinovenator, Sinusonasus, and Mei.
facts.quote: All of the sinovenatorines - Sinovenator, Sinusonasus, Mei, and Daliansaurus - lived in the Lujiatun Beds of the Yixian Formation.

facts.statement: The environment where Daliansaurus lived had cold mean annual air temperatures, reaching as low as 10°C during the Barremian and Aptian epochs.
facts.quote: Mean annual air temperatures were cold in the region during the Barremian and Aptian epochs, being as cold as 10 C.

facts.statement: Histological analysis of Daliansaurus bones indicates the individual was at least four years old when it died, based on growth lines in the radius.
facts.quote: Seasonal bone growth is apparent through the thin sections; three lines of arrested growth (LAGs) separate the cortical bone into four distinct zones within the radius, indicating that the individual was at least four years of age when it died.

facts.statement: The presence of an external fundamental system (EFS) in Daliansaurus suggests it may have reached skeletal maturity at the size of the holotype.
facts.quote: The presence of an EFS suggests minimal growth rates, indicating that the individual may have reached skeletal maturity at this size.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests Daliansaurus grew rapidly but died while still in the late subadult stage of life.
facts.quote: Overall, anatomical and histological evidence suggests that the individual grew quickly, but was only in the late subadult stage of life.

facts.statement: It is debated whether sinovenatorines like Daliansaurus coexisted strictly or replaced each other over time or were segregated by geography and ecology.
facts.quote: Rather than strict coexistence, it is possible that they replaced each other over time, or were geographically and ecologically segregated.

facts.statement: Some anatomical differences between sinovenatorines may be due to individual or ontogenetic variation rather than distinct species.
facts.quote: However, it is possible that some of these differences may arise from individual or ontogenetic variation.
